balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Amcor plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Amcor plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Amcor plc: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Amcor plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Amcor plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Amcor plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Amcor plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Amcor plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Amcor plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Amcor plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Flexibles vs Rigid Packaging
segmentRevenue.content:
Amcor reports two segments: Flexible Packaging (flexible films, laminates and packaging for food, beverage, healthcare and other end markets) and Rigid Packaging (rigid containers, mainly beverage and specialty cartons/closures).

For Amcor plc: Flexibles is roughly 70-75% of group revenue and has historically carried the more resilient healthcare and food end markets; Rigid Packaging is the smaller, more beverage-cyclical segment and the one most affected by North American beverage volumes. The FY2024/FY2025 mix shift toward Rigid Packaging follows the June 2025 completion of the Berry Global merger, which added Berry's rigid and specialty businesses.

What to watch:

  • Whether Rigid Packaging's post-merger step-up holds or is a one-off consolidation effect
  • Relative margin trends between the two segments (not shown here -- see the GAAP-vs-Adjusted chart for the blended effect)
  • Flexibles growth as the read on healthcare/food demand versus Rigid's beverage-market cyclicality

gaapVsAdjusted.title: GAAP vs Adjusted: Net income and EBITDA
gaapVsAdjusted.content:
GAAP net income and EBITDA are the statutory, audited figures. Adjusted net income and Adjusted EBITDA are Amcor's own non-GAAP measures, which add back items management considers non-operating or non-recurring -- principally restructuring, and since FY2024/FY2025, integration and transaction costs from the Berry Global merger.

For Amcor plc: the merger closed in June 2025 (Amcor's FY2025 year-end), so FY2024 and especially FY2025 GAAP results carry heavy one-off integration and transaction costs that Adjusted figures strip out. FY2025 GAAP net income ($511m) is less than half Adjusted net income ($1,136m), and GAAP EBITDA ($1,719m) sits well below Adjusted EBITDA ($2,186m) -- the gap is almost entirely merger-related, not a deterioration in the underlying packaging business.

What to watch:

  • The GAAP/Adjusted gap narrowing as integration costs roll off post-merger (expected through FY2026-FY2027)
  • Whether Adjusted EBITDA growth is organic or driven by Berry's acquired revenue base
  • Adjusted figures are management's own definition -- cross-check the addbacks disclosed in the reconciliation tables of each filing

adjustedEbitFcf.title: Adjusted EBIT and Adjusted free cash flow
adjustedEbitFcf.content:
Adjusted EBIT is Adjusted EBITDA less depreciation and amortisation. Adjusted free cash flow is management's own non-GAAP cash-generation measure, also excluding merger-related and other one-off cash costs that depress reported operating cash flow and FreeCashFlow.

For Amcor plc: like Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted net income, these are the run-rate profitability and cash-generation figures management guides to post-Berry-merger. Adjusted FCF has stayed in the $850m-950m range through FY2023-FY2025 even as GAAP FreeCashFlow and net income swung on integration costs, so it reads Amcor's underlying cash generation as more stable than GAAP alone suggests.

What to watch:

  • Adjusted FCF conversion versus Adjusted EBITDA (cash quality of the adjusted earnings)
  • Convergence of GAAP and Adjusted FCF as one-off merger costs run off
